lines.note: Continues f222's figurative 'trample somebody' expression: it is used by braggarts or others who threaten. This opening confirms that f222's low ou is a repeated catchword, not unique body text.
Fumi-tsuke means treading upon something. Pees, visibly damaged in its middle, corrects OCR pecs and supplies the expected Portuguese feet without adding an accent not clearly present.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Piſar pegandoſe algũa couſa mol-

lines.note: The scan supports Piſar pegandoſe: stepping on something soft that sticks to the feet. This resolves the OCR's Paſar pexandoſe; the initial paragraph mark is also visible and restored.

runs.text: le, & pegajoſa nos pees. ¶ Item, Per-

lines.note: Molle and pegajosa complete the description of soft sticky material. The repeated peg- in pegajoſa independently supports pegandoſe above; the next label introduces a metaphorical sense.

runs.text: met. Fazer pouco caſo, ou desprezar.

lines.note: Figuratively, treading upon somebody means making little of them or despising them. The Portuguese meaning is explicit, so it does not require a conjectural Japanese gloss.
Fumi-tsume means pressing or packing down with the feet. Arru-mar crosses the row break and is a Portuguese verb, not a separate Japanese item.
Completes arrumar com os pés, packing with the feet. The tight ospès spacing is kept as a typographic reading rather than normalized during semantic review.
Fumi-todorokashi is making a resounding noise by stamping. Todorokasu and the Portuguese fazer soar agree; the historical -aita ending is retained.
'With the feet' completes the stamping-sound definition. This is a body continuation even though it consists of only two Portuguese words.
Fumi-todome is fixing or stopping one's feet. The transitive sense distinguishes it from the following fumi-tomari, remaining in place.
Fumi-tomari means staying without proceeding further. The Portuguese construction deixar-se ficar agrees with the intransitive Japanese verb.
'Going forward' completes the negative expression: remain without advancing. It is not a new instruction to continue onward.
Fumi-wake is opening or forcing a path by walking. The ua spelling represents wa in this position, as the snow example makes clear.

The scan and context support abrindo, opening a path, and yuki wo, snow, rather than OCR abriado and Yoqi. The damaged u in Yuqi is read with support from the explicit Portuguese neve on the next row.
Completes fumi-waquru, walking through snow. The joined aneue is preserved from the print; the article and noun can be understood without altering their diplomatic spacing.
Fumi-wori is breaking something by treading on it. Uo marks wo/o, not u plus a following independent vowel in this compound.
Cane and wood illustrate objects broken by treading; ashi wo fumi-woru shifts the example to injuring one's own foot. This explains the following fall or hole.

runs.text: Entortar, ou quebrar o pès caindo, ou dando

lines.note: Twisting or breaking the foot happens by falling or stepping into a hole. The scan has lowercase caindo; the awkward printed o pès is retained rather than silently correcting its number agreement.
A hole or hollow completes the explanation of the injured foot. This continuation belongs to Fumiuori, not the next falling-down verb.
Fumi-wotoshi is making something fall by treading. The visible t and the repeated fumiuotoſu below correct OCR f in the headword; wotosu fits derrubar.
Ashi wo fumi-wotosu means losing one's footing or stepping down into empty space. The repeated verb corroborates the headword's t, while its long s remains diplomatic typography.

runs.text: Por opee em vão, & cair em baixo.

lines.note: Putting the foot into empty space and falling below explains the Japanese example. The source's opee and em baixo spacing is preserved rather than normalized.
Fumi-shibori means squeezing by treading. This is illustrated with grapes, so shiboru is pressing liquid out rather than merely crushing an object.
Budou wo fumi-shiboru means pressing grapes underfoot. The caron is retained from the scan/OCR; the Portuguese grapes below confirms the word independently of its accent shape.
Completes espremer as uvas, squeezing grapes with the feet. Initial v in vuas is ordinary historical Portuguese u/v usage and should not be mistaken for Japanese vo.
Fumi-shidaki here concerns treading on a long garment. The visible o is the article before vestido, correcting OCR e; comprido continues on the next row.

runs.text: prido, que arroja, & ſemete de baixo dos pès.

lines.note: The garment drags and gets under the feet. Arroja is retained in the source's dragging sense, rather than replaced with a modern verb chosen from the meaning.
Fumi-shitaki is presented separately from the voiced shidaki above. The printed t and separate entry are retained rather than collapsed into one normalized modern headword.
Grass and similar things illustrate treading them down. The paragraph marker then starts another example of the same action, not necessarily another headword.

The garment is trodden and crumpled underfoot. The unusual amarlotar reading is retained provisionally: the context resembles amarrotar, but that lexical expectation alone does not justify replacing the scanned consonants.
The garment is lying on the ground. This closes the preceding clause and distinguishes it from the earlier long garment being worn and dragging underfoot.
Fumi-shizume means forcing down or sinking under weight. Fundo corrects OCR furdo; the boat example below makes the sinking sense explicit.

runs.text: carregando muito os que ſe embarcão. ¶

lines.note: Those boarding overload the vessel and drive it down. Fune starts the Japanese example, which must be read with the following row rather than as a standalone headword.

Fune wo fumi-shizumete mina shinarete gozaru describes everyone dying after the overloaded boat sank. Enlarging the damaged ending supports a worn round o and final u in gozaru, not OCR gezara; the recovery is also supported by the auxiliary construction, but the weak impression remains a source of uncertainty.

Feiq. is the roman Heike citation. Enlargement supports 3 rather than OCR 2, though the numeral is worn; this is a scan reading, not verification against an edition of the cited work. Embarcação, with visible a, corrects OCR emburcação.

runs.text: no fundo os que ſe embarcarão morrerão todos.

lines.note: The people who boarded all died when they drove the boat to the bottom. Embarcarão and morrerão resolve severely broken OCR words using both the surviving letters and the connected sentence; the historical -ão past spellings are retained.
Fumi-yaburi is breaking or disrupting with the feet. Yaburu and the Portuguese quebrar/desmanchar agree; the abbreviated inflection is kept as printed.
Completes desmanchar com os pés. This is the final member of the long sequence of fumi- 'tread' compounds before the dictionary moves to fumi 'letter'.

runs.text: Recado por carta, ou que vai

lines.note: Fumi-zukai is a message by letter or its bearer. Here fumi is writing, not treading; the change of meaning is explicit in carta and the following messenger example.
Fumi-zukai wo yaru means sending a letter-bearing messenger. Mã continues into dar on the next line, and no hyphen is invented where the baseline preserves none.
Completes mandar and translates sending a message with letters. The Portuguese recado can denote the communication, while the Japanese example can focus on its carrier.
Fumi-zuki is the seventh lunar month, not July in an automatically converted Gregorian calendar. The editorial P. is italic; its period belongs to the same type run.

runs.text: Peßoa que não ſabe ler, nem eſ-

lines.note: Fumonjina is the adjective for someone unable to read or write the learned characters described next. The damaged headword is supported by Fumonjini below; Peßoa que corrects two OCR errors and supplies the singular person required by sabe.

runs.text: creuer as letras da China, & outras exquiſitas.

lines.note: The inability concerns Chinese characters and other difficult or specialized writing. Exquisitas should not be narrowed to the modern English sense 'exquisite'; the source specifies the literacy domain.
Fumonjini is the adverbial counterpart of Fumonjina. The scan has ni, not OCR mi; italic Adu. labels the grammatical function rather than supplying more Japanese.

Fumot denotes debts, glossed by oimono and a borrowed-property expression. Enlargement shows an n-like letter in xacu not, so that printed reading is retained even though shaku-motsu would be linguistically more expected. A possible printing error is not silently emended into the text.
Fumoto is the foot of a mountain or range. The tight Pède spacing is retained from the scan, and the word is distinct from the preceding final-t debt term.

runs.text: Esterco de homẽs, ou animais. ¶ Em

lines.note: Fun is dung, from humans or animals. The headword's dot is kept with its roman run; the paragraph marker introduces animal-specific terminology rather than a new alphabetical entry.

runs.text: particular o das lebres ſe diz.

lines.note: Hare droppings are called otoshi, printed Votoxi. This embedded Japanese term is roman and should remain independently switchable in the review UI.
Falcon droppings are uchi, followed by the introduction to dog droppings. The letter v in Vchi represents u; the Portuguese animal names anchor which Japanese label belongs to which animal.

Qegaxi names dog droppings, while Tame is assigned to the animals called adibes in Portuguese. The Japanese labels are retained as specialized vocabulary, without guessing a modern species equivalence for adibe.
Bird droppings are cayexi, kaeshi, then the text starts the horse category. The existing ß transcription is preserved rather than conflated with two independent long s characters.
Horse dung is coye, koe. This short continuation completes cavalos and the list, with the Japanese term in roman type rather than treating it as Portuguese.

runs.text: Hũ certo peixe de agoa doce.

lines.note: Funa is the freshwater fish, crucian carp in ordinary Japanese usage. The source gives only a certain freshwater fish, so its brief gloss is not expanded into a modern species identification in the transcription.
Funa-agari wo suru means disembarking. Funa- is now the combining form of boat, distinct from the preceding fish headword despite identical letters.
After disembarking one retires to a house or other place. Recolher-se supplies that movement ashore, not the sense of collecting cargo.
'Or place' completes the destination after disembarkation. The short continuation stays attached to the explanation of funa-agari.

runs.text: Folguedo por mar, ou por rio.

lines.note: Funa-asobi is boating for pleasure on sea or river. Folguedo marks recreation, rather than boat work or a technical naval exercise.
Funaba is a harbour or anchorage; Cami introduces a regional synonym used in the upper/capital region. The scan's upright Cami is kept as embedded Japanese rather than italic Portuguese.
Funatsuki is the regional synonym. The next example offers funaba or funatsuki as alternatives before no yoi tokoro, a good place for vessels to lie.
Completes funatsuki no yoi tokoro, a good anchorage. Surgir is Portuguese nautical anchoring here, not the ordinary modern sense of appearing.
Ancorar and bom porto make the anchorage sense explicit. This confirms the nautical meaning of surgir on the preceding row.

runs.text: Bancos da galè, ou outra embarca-

lines.note: Funabari denotes transverse benches or timbers in a vessel. The first Portuguese sense specifies a galley's rowing benches, and the next extends it to other crosspieces.

runs.text: ção onde ſe aßentão pera remar. ¶ Itẽ, Fei

lines.note: The benches are where rowers sit. Fei- continues into chos as a second nautical sense; the existing no-hyphen transcription is not changed merely because the word crosses a row.

runs.text: chos. i, paos atraueſados onde ſe encoſtão na

lines.note: The crosspieces are explained as transverse timbers against which people lean. The beginning of atraueſados is obscured by a dark blemish; surviving letters and the transverse-timber sense support this qualified recovery over OCR acaueſados.
'In the vessel' completes the crosspiece definition. It is not an additional Japanese entry despite occupying a short independent row.
Funabata is the side or edge of a boat. Nauio corrects OCR vauio; its initial n is visible and the Portuguese gloss directly supports the vessel edge.
Funa-bashi is a bridge of boats. The worn headword's u and a are supported by its clear repetition in the next example and by ponte; OCR Fanabixi obscured this ordinary compound.
Funa-bashi wo kakuru means constructing a boat bridge. Fazer, with visible a, is the infinitive matching the example, not OCR Fizer.
The bridge consists of boats tied to one another. The damaged b in embarcaçoẽs was lost by OCR and replaced with a gap; the scan supports restoring the word.

runs.text: Portador por mar, ou occaſião de

lines.note: Funabin is a sea-going carrier or an opportunity to send something by boat. The visibly roman Fu continues into ne on the next row; this embedded Japanese fune should not be swallowed by the italic Portuguese run.

Completes the embedded fune, 'boat', and the opportunity that presents itself. The continuation ne looks more slanted than the preceding Fu; its OCR italic style is retained and both fragments remain available for typeface review.
Funa-bito are sailors or people of the sea. The visible n and the boat-person compound correct OCR Fumabito; there is no need to replace the historical bito with modern hito.
Funa-kage is the silhouette or appearance of a vessel. Gue represents ge, fitting kage rather than an unrelated sound sequence.
The vessel appears in the distance. This clarifies that sombra can mean a distant outline, not only a shadow cast on the water.
Funa-kazu is the number of vessels. Kazu corresponds directly to numero, providing a straightforward semantic check on the Japanese compound.
Funako denotes sailors or rowers. The worn headword is read with c, not OCR x, and remeiros restores the recognizable rower term from the scan; both fit the boat-worker meaning.

Funakuji is an anchorage charge or service in this context; Portuguese ancoragem alone is brief enough that its precise scope should not be over-specified. The Japanese kuji is retained rather than confused with a lottery word.

runs.text: Portador por mar, ou occaſião q̃

lines.note: Funa-dayori is a maritime carrier or opportunity for sending something, parallel to funabin above. The Portuguese q̃ abbreviation is not expanded in Level 1.
'That presents itself by sea' completes the available-carrier sense. The double f in offerece belongs to the printed historical spelling.

Funa-dougu means ship's equipment or fittings. Petrechos, supported by the visible t, corrects OCR perrechos; the caron in the Japanese headword is retained without attempting phonological normalization.

runs.text: O deter as embarcaçoẽs q̃ nenhũa

lines.note: Funa-dome is detention of vessels so none can leave port. This is an embargo or departure prohibition, not merely stopping one boat physically.
Funadome de aru means that a departure ban is in force. The Portuguese then starts haver, describing the existence of the prohibition rather than the vessel's motion.

The lord's prohibition prevents vessels leaving port. Tono is visibly upright embedded Japanese and is restored to roman type, with a UI toggle available rather than relying on a capitalization rule alone.
Completes saia and the ban on a vessel departing the port. The y spelling in this Portuguese verb is preserved as printed.

Funa-gakoi is equated with fune wo kakou koto, enclosing or protecting a boat. The visible e corrects OCR Funcuo; the following defence against enemy weapons supports protective enclosure rather than ordinary maintenance alone.

runs.text: da embarcação pera que ſe não tome dos inimi

lines.note: The vessel is arranged so enemies cannot capture it. The broken inimigos crosses the row boundary; no division mark is added merely from grammatical expectation.

runs.text: gos, ou não receba dano das frechas, armas, &c.

lines.note: Protection from arrows and weapons further defines the enclosure. Frechas is the printed historical Portuguese form, not silently changed to modern flechas.
Funaji is a sea route. Gi corresponds to ji in this spelling system, so a kana hint with gi would obscure the ordinary Japanese word for a voyage route.
Funa-gokochi is the sensation of being seasick. The damaged initial F is confirmed by the repeated examples below and the NINJAL headword list; OCR lowercase r would produce an unrelated form.

runs.text: mo quãdo hum estaua na embarcação. ¶

lines.note: The sensation resembles being aboard a vessel. The next example begins Fu-nagocochi across the row; its classification is Japanese even though the preceding discussion is Portuguese.

runs.text: nagocochi ga aru, l, funagocochide goza-

lines.note: Funa-gokochi ga aru or funagokochi de gozaru describe having that lingering shipboard sensation. The two equivalent constructions and the next row's ru complete a coherent Japanese example.

runs.text: Eſtar ainda de pois de deſembarcado como

lines.note: Completes gozaru and explains feeling the effect even after disembarking. The separated de pois is preserved as printed, not joined automatically to modern depois.
The person remains queasy or dazed from the boat. Fune is embedded Japanese in an otherwise Portuguese explanation and looks italic here; that style is retained with a UI toggle for human review.
